processing: As with other Yunnan raw pu-erh, the leaf is typically wilted, wok-fired, rolled and sun-dried into mao cha, then sold loose or steamed and pressed; no ripe-style pile fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as is usual for Mengku raw pu-erh; little is documented about the season here beyond that.
appearance_dry: Typical of Mengku large-leaf raw tea: long, thick dark green strands with some pale tip.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear golden yellow when young.
appearance_wet: Thick large leaves in olive green, as with other Mengku raw teas.
taste_profile: Little is documented about Baka's own taste. Mengku raw tea in general is sweet, fragrant and vigorous, and plantation leaf tends to be simpler than old-tree leaf.

brewing.notes: General Mengku raw settings, since nothing specific to Baka is recorded. Shorten the early steeps if it turns bitter.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year like other sheng: mostly as spring tea of a stated year, either as loose mao cha or pressed cakes. Young cakes of one to three years are the usual purchase, and those who store it age it for a decade or more. Ask for the year and the tree age, since old-tree and plantation leaf are priced far apart.
description:
Baka is a high tea village on Mengku's western half-mountain, nearly 2,000 metres up and facing the Bangma Snow Mountain. It is one of the ten small western areas in the group called the Mengku Eighteen Villages, on the same side of the mountain as Bingdao but far less famous.

Three hamlets make up the village, Shangzhai, Zhongzhai and Xiazhai, most households Han. Nearly all the tea is relatively young plantation; only a small remnant of old garden survives, mainly around Xiazhai. That matters when you buy, because old-tree Baka should be scarce.

No detailed tasting record for Baka stands out, so expect what is typical of Mengku raw tea: thick leaf, sweetness and some force. Brew it as you would any strong young sheng, with short steeps.

When buying, ask whether the leaf is plantation or old-tree, and be careful with large claims of old-tree Baka.
history: There were few tea gardens here in 1950. New planting began around 1960 and continued into the 1980s, and for a long time the leaf went to the primary processing station at Dongguo. Poor roads and little outside contact kept the price low.
